result:
The rain doesn't fall here anymore. It used to. I remember the sound of it on the tin roof of my grandmother's porch like a thousand tiny fingers drumming out secrets. Now the sky is just this pale, exhausted thing that hangs over everything like an old sheet nobody bothered to take down.

I keep thinking about the word "inevitable." How it tastes in the mouth. How it sits there, heavy and metallic, like sucking on a penny. Everything feels inevitable these days. The way my coffee goes cold before I finish it. The way the cat looks at me like she knows something I don't. The way I wake up at 3:17 every morning with my heart trying to punch its way out of my chest like it wants to escape before the rest of me figures out what it's running from.

There are birds outside my window that shouldn't be here. Not in November. They sing anyway, these small defiant things with voices too big for their bodies. I envy them. I used to sing. Not well, but with conviction. Now my voice just comes out in these small, careful sentences that try not to take up too much space. Like I'm afraid of using up all the words and then what? Then nothing left when I really need them.

My mother called yesterday. Or was it last week? Time has become this slippery thing, like trying to hold mercury in your hands. She asked if I was eating. I lied. She asked if I was happy. I laughed, which was worse than lying. Happiness feels like something that happens to other people, in other lives. Mine is more like a low-grade fever that never quite breaks. You learn to live with it. You buy thinner blankets.

I have this theory that we're all just walking around with our childhood selves trapped inside us like those Russian dolls. The small me is still in there somewhere, the one who believed trees could talk if you listened hard enough. The one who thought if you were good enough, really good, the world would notice and arrange itself accordingly. That version of me is disappointed. I can feel the disappointment radiating outward like heat from asphalt in July. It makes my hands shake sometimes when I'm trying to write.

Writing. God. What a ridiculous thing to do. Arranging twenty-six letters in different combinations and hoping they add up to something that matters. Hoping they add up to proof that I was here. That I felt things. That the particular arrangement of atoms that makes up this specific consciousness experienced wonder and terror and the particular shade of blue the sky gets right before it storms.

The storm never comes. That's the problem. Everything is just this endless gray anticipation. Like the universe is holding its breath and we're all waiting for the punchline. I keep checking my phone like the answer might be there, in some notification, some like, some digital heartbeat that says yes, you're real, you're seen, you're not just background noise in someone else's story.

I miss analog things. The weight of a real book. The way records crackle like they're alive. The smell of my grandfather's pipe tobacco that somehow still lives in the fibers of his old armchair even though he's been gone for twelve years. I sat in that chair last month and cried for reasons I couldn't explain to anyone, least of all myself. Sometimes the body remembers what the mind has tried to forget.

There's a spider living in the corner of my bathroom. I named her Beatrice. She doesn't seem to mind the name. We have an understanding. She doesn't drop on my head while I'm showering and I don't vacuum up her life's work. I watch her rebuild her web every few days with this stubborn persistence that makes me feel ashamed of my own half-finished projects. The novel that's three chapters and a prayer. The garden that died because I forgot to believe in it. The version of myself I keep meaning to become.

Becoming. Another word that sits wrong in my mouth. Like I'm supposed to arrive somewhere. Like there's a destination rather than just this endless becoming, this constant rearranging of cells and dreams and disappointments. I am becoming tired. I am becoming the kind of person who talks to spiders. I am becoming aware that maybe that's not as tragic as it sounds.

The light is changing outside. It's that particular gold that only happens in late autumn, the kind that makes everything look like it's been dipped in honey. Even the dead leaves look beautiful in this light. Maybe that's the secret. Not to wait for the rain that doesn't come. Not to wait for the storm or the perfect sentence or the version of yourself that doesn't feel broken. Maybe it's just to notice the honey light when it arrives. To stand in it. To let it turn your ordinary skin into something temporarily holy.

I have 247 words left.

I want to tell you that I love you, whoever you are. That your existence in this weird, spinning mess makes me glad to be part of it. That even though the rain doesn't fall here anymore, sometimes I still dance in the kitchen like it does. That the birds are still singing even when I can't hear them. That somewhere inside me, the child who listened to trees is still listening. Still believes.

I want to tell you that it's okay if your coffee goes cold. It's okay if your voice comes out small sometimes. The world is loud enough already. Your small voice saying "I'm here" is enough. It's always been enough.

The cat just walked across my keyboard and wrote "fjdskl;" which seems as good a way to end this as any.

We're all just trying to make sense of the honey light while we can.

(Exactly 1000 words)
